title: Cauchy-Schwarz and Holder: check exponents and measure normalization
before: Cauchy-Schwarz: |E[XY]| <= (E X^2)^{1/2} (E Y^2)^{1/2}; the sum form (sum a_i b_i)^2 <= (sum a_i^2)(sum b_i^2), and sum_{i=1}^N a_i <= sqrt(N) (sum a_i^2)^{1/2}. Holder: E|XY| <= ||X||_p ||Y||_q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. A step whose exponents do not sum to one, or that bounds a sum of N terms by (sum a_i^2)^{1/2} without the sqrt(N) factor, has the constant wrong.
after: Cauchy-Schwarz: |E[XY]| <= (E X^2)^(1/2) (E Y^2)^(1/2). For finite sums, (sum a_i b_i)^2 <= (sum a_i^2)(sum b_i^2), hence sum_{i=1}^N a_i <= sqrt(N)(sum a_i^2)^(1/2); the sqrt(N) factor cannot generally be dropped. The standard two-factor Holder theorem uses conjugate exponents p,q in [1,infinity], 1/p + 1/q = 1. This is not a necessary condition for every bound with constant one. On a probability space, 1/p + 1/q <= 1 also gives E|XY| <= ||X||_p ||Y||_q for measurable X,Y with finite indicated norms, by Holder plus probability-space Lp embeddings. For example p=2,q=3 is valid. On a measure space of finite mass M>0, the corresponding bound is integral |fg| <= M^(1-1/p-1/q) ||f||_p ||g||_q when 1/p+1/q<=1 (with 1/infinity=0). Do not omit that factor on an unnormalised space. If 1/p+1/q>1, a concentrated indicator on a probability space refutes a universal constant-one bound. Check the measure, exponents and an actual justification before rejecting a step.

title: Monotone convergence vs dominated convergence vs Fatou
before: Monotone convergence: 0 <= X_n increasing to X gives E X_n -> E X, with no integrability assumption (the limit may be infinite). Dominated convergence: X_n -> X a.s. and |X_n| <= Y with E Y < infinity gives E X_n -> E X; it needs the DOMINATOR, and cannot be used to prove that E X is finite when finiteness of E X is the claim. Fatou: E liminf X_n <= liminf E X_n for X_n >= 0 (the expectation of the liminf is the SMALLER side). A monotone nonnegative sequence with no known integrable bound calls for monotone convergence, not dominated convergence.
after: Monotone convergence: 0 <= X_n increasing to X gives E X_n -> E X, with no integrability assumption (the limit may be infinite). Dominated convergence: X_n -> X a.s. and |X_n| <= Y with E Y < infinity gives E X_n -> E X; the dominator's integrability must be established independently. These hypotheses imply that X is integrable, so dominated convergence can establish finiteness of E X. Circularity arises only if integrability of the proposed dominator relies on the unproved conclusion. Fatou: E liminf X_n <= liminf E X_n for X_n >= 0 (the expectation of the liminf is the SMALLER side). A monotone nonnegative sequence with no known integrable bound calls for monotone convergence, not dominated convergence.

title: Fubini-Tonelli: swapping integrals needs nonnegativity or absolute integrability
before: Tonelli: for nonnegative measurable f the iterated integrals agree with the product integral, always. Fubini: for signed f, the swap needs the integral of |f| over the product to be finite. A step that exchanges a sum and an integral, or two expectations, for a signed integrand with no absolute-integrability check is a gap; a step that does it for nonnegative terms is fine.
after: On a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, Tonelli identifies the iterated and product integrals of a nonnegative measurable function, possibly with value infinity. For an absolutely integrable signed function, Fubini identifies the finite iterated and product integrals. Check the measure-space and measurability hypotheses as well as sign or absolute integrability before invoking these theorems. The absence of absolute integrability prevents this standard Fubini justification; it does not by itself prove that two particular iterated integrals differ. They can agree by a separate direct argument even when the signed product integral is undefined. Never infer existence of that product integral from cancellation in the iterated integrals.

title: limsup and liminf: what each bounds
before: liminf a_n <= limsup a_n always; a bound limsup a_n <= C means eventually a_n <= C + eps, a bound liminf a_n >= c means eventually a_n >= c - eps. limsup(a_n + b_n) <= limsup a_n + limsup b_n; liminf(a_n + b_n) >= liminf a_n + liminf b_n; the reverse inequalities are false in general. A chain that replaces a limsup by a liminf on the LARGER side of an inequality is a non sequitur unless the limit exists.
after: liminf a_n <= limsup a_n always; a bound limsup a_n <= C means eventually a_n <= C + eps, a bound liminf a_n >= c means eventually a_n >= c - eps. limsup(a_n + b_n) <= limsup a_n + limsup b_n; liminf(a_n + b_n) >= liminf a_n + liminf b_n; the reverse inequalities are false in general. Replacing a limsup by a liminf on the larger side strengthens an inequality and is not justified by the original bound alone. It may be justified by an independent stronger bound; convergence is sufficient but not necessary.

title: Fubini vs Tonelli: Tonelli needs nonnegativity, Fubini needs absolute integrability
before: Tonelli: for a NONNEGATIVE measurable f on a product of sigma-finite spaces the iterated integrals equal the double integral (possibly +infinity). Fubini: if int int |f| < infinity (checked by Tonelli), the iterated integrals exist, are finite, and agree. Sigma-finiteness of BOTH measures is a hypothesis (counting measure on [0,1] is the standard counterexample). Exchanging a sum and an integral, or an expectation and a sum, IS Fubini-Tonelli: it needs nonnegative terms or a finite sum of absolute values. A step that swaps E and sum for signed summands with no absolute bound, or swaps limit and integral by 'Fubini', is where the error usually sits.
after: Tonelli: for a NONNEGATIVE measurable f on a product of sigma-finite spaces the iterated integrals equal the double integral (possibly +infinity). Fubini: if int int |f| < infinity (checked by Tonelli), the iterated integrals exist, are finite, and agree. Sigma-finiteness of BOTH measures is a hypothesis (counting measure on [0,1] is the standard counterexample). Fubini-Tonelli is a standard justification for exchanging an infinite sum and an integral: nonnegative summands suffice for Tonelli, while integrability of the sum of absolute values suffices for Fubini. A finite sum of integrable signed terms uses linearity. Particular iterated integrals can also agree by an independent argument without absolute integrability; do not confuse absence of this sufficient theorem with proof that every swap is invalid. A step that swaps E and sum for signed summands with no absolute bound, or swaps limit and integral by 'Fubini', is where the error usually sits.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz and Holder: conjugate form, probability embeddings, and direction
before: Cauchy-Schwarz: |E[XY]| <= (E X^2)^{1/2} (E Y^2)^{1/2}; sum |a_i b_i| <= (sum a_i^2)^{1/2} (sum b_i^2)^{1/2}; equality iff proportional. Holder: E|XY| <= ||X||_p ||Y||_q with 1/p + 1/q = 1, p,q in [1, infinity]; generalized to 1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k = 1. Reverse Holder needs p < 1 with the conjugate exponent negative, and positive factors. The typical wrong step writes exponents that do not sum to one (e.g. 1/2 with 1/3), squares only one factor, applies Holder to get an upper bound on a PRODUCT of norms from a norm of a product (that direction is false), or uses Cauchy-Schwarz for E[XY] >= .... Check: the two exponents on the right must satisfy 1/p + 1/q = 1 exactly.
after: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds |E[XY]| above by ||X||_2 ||Y||_2, and sum |a_i b_i| above by (sum a_i^2)^(1/2)(sum b_i^2)^(1/2). The standard two-factor Holder theorem uses conjugate exponents p,q in [1,infinity], 1/p + 1/q = 1. This is not a necessary condition for every bound with constant one. On a probability space, 1/p + 1/q <= 1 also gives E|XY| <= ||X||_p ||Y||_q for measurable X,Y with finite indicated norms, by Holder plus probability-space Lp embeddings. For example p=2,q=3 is valid. On a measure space of finite mass M>0, the corresponding bound is integral |fg| <= M^(1-1/p-1/q) ||f||_p ||g||_q when 1/p+1/q<=1 (with 1/infinity=0). Do not omit that factor on an unnormalised space. If 1/p+1/q>1, a concentrated indicator on a probability space refutes a universal constant-one bound. Check the measure, exponents and an actual justification before rejecting a step. The usual Holder upper bound does not reverse to bound a product of norms above by the norm or integral of the product: disjointly supported nonzero functions refute that reversal. Reverse-Holder statements for exponents below one use different hypotheses, including positivity, and require their own justification. Also check that squaring or taking a root is applied to every required factor.

title: Portmanteau theorem: equivalent forms of weak convergence and the direction for open and closed sets
before: mu_n => mu iff any of: int f dmu_n -> int f dmu for all bounded CONTINUOUS f; limsup mu_n(F) <= mu(F) for all CLOSED F; liminf mu_n(G) >= mu(G) for all OPEN G; mu_n(A) -> mu(A) for all mu-continuity sets (mu(boundary A) = 0); int f dmu_n -> int f dmu for bounded Lipschitz f. The directions pair with the topology: closed sets with limsup and '<=', open sets with liminf and '>='. Weak convergence does NOT give convergence of mu_n(A) for an arbitrary Borel A, nor of int f dmu_n for unbounded f (that needs uniform integrability) or discontinuous f. A step with 'limsup mu_n(G) <= mu(G) for open G', or 'liminf on closed sets', or convergence of expectations of an unbounded functional without a moment bound, is the defect.
after: For Borel probability measures on a common metric space, weak convergence mu_n => mu is characterized by convergence of integrals of every bounded continuous real function. Equivalent Portmanteau forms are limsup mu_n(F) <= mu(F) for every closed F; liminf mu_n(G) >= mu(G) for every open G; convergence mu_n(A) -> mu(A) for every Borel mu-continuity set A; and convergence of integrals of every bounded Lipschitz function. Preserve the set class and inequality direction. Weak convergence alone does not guarantee convergence on an arbitrary Borel set or of expectations of an arbitrary unbounded continuous functional. Uniform integrability of the functional values is a standard sufficient upgrade, not a necessary condition for convergence of signed expectations: cancellation can give the expectation limit without uniform integrability. A discontinuous functional can also be admissible under additional hypotheses, such as a discontinuity set of limiting measure zero in the bounded case. Check the argument that justifies the particular expectation or set limit; absence of one familiar sufficient condition does not by itself identify an error.

title: Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality and the Wasserstein distances: W_1 is a sup over 1-Lipschitz functions; W_p increases in p
before: W_1(mu, nu) = sup{ int f dmu - int f dnu : f 1-Lipschitz } = inf over couplings E|X - Y|. W_p = (inf over couplings E|X-Y|^p)^{1/p} is nondecreasing in p (W_1 <= W_2 <= ... on the same space), so an upper bound on W_2 bounds W_1 but not conversely; W_p metrises weak convergence PLUS convergence of p-th moments. Total variation and W_1: on a space of diameter D, W_1 <= D . TV; TV is not bounded by W_1 in general. Wrong steps: sup over Lipschitz functions with constant L without the factor L; W_2 <= W_1 (backwards); weak convergence claimed from W_p convergence without noting it is stronger, or W_p convergence claimed from weak convergence without the moment condition; the inf over couplings written as a sup.
after: W_1(mu, nu) = sup{ int f dmu - int f dnu : f 1-Lipschitz } = inf over couplings E|X - Y|. W_p = (inf over couplings E|X-Y|^p)^{1/p} is nondecreasing in p (W_1 <= W_2 <= ... on the same space), so an upper bound on W_2 bounds W_1 but not conversely; W_p metrises weak convergence PLUS convergence of p-th moments. Total variation and W_1: on a space of diameter D, W_1 <= D . TV; TV is not bounded by W_1 in general. Wrong steps: sup over Lipschitz functions with constant L without the factor L; W_2 <= W_1 (backwards); W_p convergence implies weak convergence in the standard probability-measure setting; using this implication does not require a separate comment that it is stronger. Conversely, weak convergence alone does not generally imply W_p convergence; check p-th moment convergence or another sufficient argument; the inf over couplings written as a sup.

title: Levy's continuity theorem and Cramer-Wold: characteristic functions and weak convergence
before: If phi_n(t) -> phi(t) for every t and phi is CONTINUOUS AT 0, then phi is the characteristic function of a law mu and mu_n => mu; conversely mu_n => mu gives phi_n -> phi uniformly on compacts. Continuity at 0 is the tightness condition: pointwise convergence to a function discontinuous at 0 (e.g. N(0, n)) gives no weak limit. Cramer-Wold: X_n => X in R^d iff <t, X_n> => <t, X> for every t in R^d. Uniqueness: equal characteristic functions give equal laws; a characteristic function determines the law but need not be integrable (inversion with a density needs phi in L^1). Wrong steps: the limit phi assumed to be a characteristic function without continuity at 0; one-dimensional convergence of each coordinate offered for joint convergence (that needs ALL linear combinations); the mgf used where it may be infinite.
after: If phi_n(t) -> phi(t) for every t and phi is CONTINUOUS AT 0, then phi is the characteristic function of a law mu and mu_n => mu; conversely mu_n => mu gives phi_n -> phi uniformly on compacts. Continuity at 0 is the tightness condition: pointwise convergence to a function discontinuous at 0 (e.g. N(0, n)) gives no weak limit. Cramer-Wold: X_n => X in R^d iff <t, X_n> => <t, X> for every t in R^d. Uniqueness: equal characteristic functions give equal laws; a characteristic function determines the law. If phi is in L^1, Fourier inversion gives a bounded continuous density through an absolutely convergent integral. This is a sufficient theorem: existence of a density does not imply phi is in L^1 (a uniform law has a sinc characteristic function). Other inversion formulas or limiting interpretations require their own justification. Wrong steps: the limit phi assumed to be a characteristic function without continuity at 0; one-dimensional convergence of each coordinate offered for joint convergence (that needs ALL linear combinations); the mgf used where it may be infinite.

title: Convergence modes: a.s., in probability, in L^p, in distribution - which implies which and what upgrades need
before: a.s. => in probability => in distribution; L^p => in probability (and L^q for q < p on a probability space); in probability => a.s. along a SUBSEQUENCE (not the full sequence); in distribution to a CONSTANT => in probability; in probability + UI => L^1; in probability + domination => L^p. Not implied: a.s. from in probability (1_{[k/2^n,(k+1)/2^n]} typewriter sequence); L^p from a.s. (needs UI/domination); a.s. from L^p (needs a summable rate, e.g. sum E|X_n - X|^p < infinity via Borel-Cantelli); convergence of expectations from any mode without integrability control. Uniform convergence of functions is stronger than pointwise; convergence of CDFs at continuity points is exactly weak convergence. A step that writes 'in probability, hence almost surely' (without a subsequence or a summable rate), 'in distribution hence in probability' (with a non-constant limit), or 'a.s. hence in L^1' (with no dominator) alters one word and breaks.
after: For real random variables on a probability space: a.s. convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution. For finite p >= 1, L^p convergence implies convergence in probability and in L^q for 1 <= q < p; in particular it already gives convergence of expectations. Convergence in probability has an a.s.-convergent subsequence, but does not generally give a.s. convergence of the full sequence. Convergence in distribution to a constant implies convergence in probability. For finite p >= 1, convergence in probability together with uniform integrability of {|X_n|^p} gives L^p convergence. A common dominator D with |X_n| <= D and E[D^p] < infinity is sufficient; an L^1 dominator alone does not give L^2 convergence. These statements do not assert L^infinity convergence. L^p convergence alone need not imply a.s. convergence: sum E|X_n-X|^p < infinity is one sufficient Borel-Cantelli condition, not a necessary rate. A.s. convergence plus uniform integrability gives L^1 convergence even when no integrable common dominator exists. Check the actual hypotheses before rejecting an upgrade: a missing sufficient condition does not rule out another valid argument. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence; for real-valued laws, convergence of CDFs at continuity points of the limiting CDF characterizes convergence in distribution.

title: Markov and Chebyshev inequalities: which side of t, which power, and where the moment sits
before: Markov: for X >= 0 and t > 0, P(X >= t) <= E[X]/t. The expectation is in the numerator and the threshold in the denominator; inverting them, or writing P(X <= t) on the left, is a fatal one-token change. Applying it to |X|^p gives P(|X| >= t) <= E[|X|^p]/t^p, and the exponent p must appear on BOTH sides: E[|X|^p]/t is wrong. Chebyshev is the p = 2 centred case, P(|X - E X| >= t) <= Var(X)/t^2, and in the k-standard-deviation form P(|X - E X| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2; writing 1/k or sigma^2/t is the usual corruption. The exponential (Chernoff) form is P(X >= t) <= e^{-lam t} E[e^{lam X}] for every lam > 0, and one then optimises over lam; the sign in the exponent must make e^{-lam t} decay, and for the lower tail P(X <= t) one uses lam < 0, i.e. e^{lam t} E[e^{-lam X}]. Markov requires nonnegativity, not integrability alone, and requires no independence or distributional assumption. It is a bound in one direction only: it never lower-bounds a tail, so a step that deduces P(X >= t) >= something from Markov has flipped the inequality. Note also the layer-cake link: Markov is exactly the statement that t P(X >= t) <= int_{X >= t} X dmu <= E[X].
after: Markov: for X >= 0 and t > 0, P(X >= t) <= E[X]/t. The expectation is in the numerator and the threshold in the denominator; inverting them, or writing P(X <= t) on the left, is a fatal one-token change. Applying it to |X|^p gives P(|X| >= t) <= E[|X|^p]/t^p, and the exponent p must appear on BOTH sides: E[|X|^p]/t is wrong. Chebyshev is the p = 2 centred case, P(|X - E X| >= t) <= Var(X)/t^2, and in the k-standard-deviation form P(|X - E X| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2; writing 1/k or sigma^2/t is the usual corruption. The exponential (Chernoff) form is P(X >= t) <= e^{-lam t} E[e^{lam X}] for every lam > 0, and one then optimises over lam; the sign in the exponent must make e^{-lam t} decay, and for the lower tail P(X <= t), lam < 0 gives the upper bound e^{-lam t} E[e^{lam X}]. Equivalently, with s > 0 use e^{s t} E[e^{-s X}]. Markov requires nonnegativity, not integrability alone, and requires no independence or distributional assumption. It is a bound in one direction only: it never lower-bounds a tail, so a step that deduces P(X >= t) >= something from Markov has flipped the inequality. Note also the layer-cake link: Markov is exactly the statement that t P(X >= t) <= int_{X >= t} X dmu <= E[X].

title: Holder, Minkowski and Jensen: which exponent goes on which factor and which way the convexity runs
before: Holder: int |f g| dmu <= ||f||_p ||g||_q with 1/p + 1/q = 1, 1 <= p <= infinity. The exponents are conjugate, not equal, and the inequality bounds the integral of the product by the product of the norms, never the reverse; Cauchy-Schwarz is p = q = 2. Minkowski is the triangle inequality ||f + g||_p <= ||f||_p + ||g||_p, valid for p >= 1 and FAILING for 0 < p < 1, where for NONNEGATIVE f and g it reverses, ||f + g||_p >= ||f||_p + ||g||_p; so quoting it at p < 1 in the usual direction is false, and quoting the reversal without f, g >= 0 is a dropped hypothesis. Minkowski's integral inequality moves a norm inside an integral, || int f(., y) dnu(y) ||_p <= int ||f(., y)||_p dnu(y), and the direction (norm of the integral <= integral of the norm) must not be exchanged. Jensen: for a convex phi and a probability measure, phi(E[X]) <= E[phi(X)]; for concave phi the inequality flips. The probability normalisation is essential, and on a general measure space Jensen requires mu(S) = 1 or an explicit averaging. The conditional form E[phi(X) | G] >= phi(E[X | G]) a.s. keeps the same direction. Consequences whose direction is often corrupted: t -> ||X||_t is nondecreasing in t on a probability space, so ||X||_1 <= ||X||_2 <= ||X||_infinity, and Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 >= 0 is the p = 2 instance.
after: Holder: int |f g| dmu <= ||f||_p ||g||_q with 1/p + 1/q = 1, 1 <= p <= infinity. This states the standard conjugate-exponent version; p = q = 2 gives Cauchy-Schwarz. Other exponent pairs can give valid bounds through Lp embeddings: on a probability space, 1/p+1/q <= 1 suffices for the same upper bound, while a finite unnormalised measure contributes the factor mu(S)^(1-1/p-1/q). A nonconjugate pair is not automatically an error. The usual upper bound does not reverse without additional hypotheses. Minkowski's integral inequality moves a norm inside an integral, || int f(., y) dnu(y) ||_p <= int ||f(., y)||_p dnu(y), and the direction (norm of the integral <= integral of the norm) must not be exchanged. Jensen: for a convex phi and a probability measure, phi(E[X]) <= E[phi(X)]; for concave phi the inequality flips. The probability normalisation is essential, and on a general measure space Jensen requires mu(S) = 1 or an explicit averaging. The conditional form E[phi(X) | G] >= phi(E[X | G]) a.s. keeps the same direction. Consequences whose direction is often corrupted: t -> ||X||_t is nondecreasing in t on a probability space, so ||X||_1 <= ||X||_2 <= ||X||_infinity, and Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 >= 0 is the p = 2 instance.
